name: Aisha Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for a side. This is confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Aisha Santos, 58, and I came into building work late after the laundry closed. I'm a junior hand even though my hair says otherwise; I carry boards, mark cuts and help with framing while I learn from the qualified crew. I left school early, so I like getting a straight edge right with my hands. The early start suits me, but hauling sheets and waiting to hear whether there's work next week wear me down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a clever phone won't lift a sheet of plywood for us. If the new ordering screen saves someone ten minutes, fine, but we still have to measure the opening twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm worried even without a robot. I'm 58, still the junior hand on a lot of jobs, and one wet month would empty what little cash my partner Elena and I have. My knees don't give me a pension just because they're sore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking the carpentry and general labour shifts I'm offered, starting Monday with the frame job on Willow Road. I'd put twenty from each full week's pay into a separate account whenever the hours allow it. In the first year of this mild change I'd use the AI app I already use to check material lists, but I'd still measure myself before a cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel wound tight about the bills, though the AI part doesn't frighten me much. I can breathe when a full week of work lands. I can't count on four full weeks in a row.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last month the rain stopped the roof job for three days. Did that change how you see a quiet AI future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, those three days came straight out of the food money. Elena works part time at the laundry, but her hours move around too. That's why I call the plateau uneasy, not restful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned using an app every day. What does it actually help with on site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I ask it to turn a rough list of timber lengths into a tidy order before I show the foreman. It once missed the offcuts we could reuse, so I caught it with my pencil. I like a tool that admits I still have to look.

say: I would tell the **crew** that small software gains still leave us cutting and carrying timber.
I would say a **measurement** needs a person to check it before anyone orders wood.
think: I have less than a **month saved**, and a rainy week already threatens our food budget.
My **junior place** and sore knees worry me more than mild AI changes.
do: Keep taking **site shifts** on Willow Road and other local jobs.
Transfer **twenty** from each full week of pay when hours allow.
Check **material lists** with my AI app before measuring by hand.
feel: I feel **anxious** about uneven hours and bills, though the AI change itself feels small.
S0.quote: My knees don't give me a pension just because they're sore.
fieldNote: Aisha frames the **plateau** through lost workdays and cash, rather than through a threat from software.
Her daily AI use has a **practical limit**: she checks output against site measurements and salvageable timber.

steps.text: Take carpentry and labour shifts on the Willow Road frame job
Put twenty from each full week of pay into a separate account
Check timber orders with the AI app and measure cuts by hand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the office will feel this before the saw benches do. If software writes the bids and buys the timber, the foreman should show us where the saved hours go. I wouldn't cheer while the agency workers lose their calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think our small contractor could start quoting more jobs with fewer office staff, then push the site crew to finish faster. I'm low in the pecking order, so a quiet week could become a quiet month. The slow robots might reach repetitive fitting before I can retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask the site steward about joining the builders' union, and I'd sign up if the dues fit a work week. I'd also learn the firm's digital cutting sheets from Mara, our foreman, because I already use AI but I don't know that system. In the first year after the change shows up, I'd still seek paid site days and apply to the two repair crews across town if our rota thins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm curious about a better way to avoid waste. I'm also anxious when people say efficiency and mean fewer names on Friday's schedule. Both feelings turn up when I open the work group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask Mara at the next toolbox meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my foreman Mara whether saved office time means more bids or fewer site hours. She may not know, but I want the answer said in front of everyone. The youngest agency lads won't risk asking first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd join a union and apply elsewhere. Which happens first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The steward gets the first conversation this Friday, because I can do that without leaving a paying shift. If the rota drops for two weeks, I'll send applications to the repair crews. I'd rather repair old houses than chase a robot round a new one.

say: I would tell the **crew** that software may reach bids and orders before it reaches our saws.
I would ask where the **saved hours** go before celebrating faster quotes.
think: I fear a **smaller rota** for junior site workers when the contractor speeds up.
My **retirement** could still be too far away if repetitive fitting becomes automated.
do: Ask the **steward** about union dues and join if a work week covers them.
Learn **digital cutting sheets** from my foreman Mara.
Apply to **repair crews** across town after two thin rota weeks.
feel: I feel **curious** about less waste and anxious about fewer shifts.
S1.quote: I'd rather repair old houses than chase a robot round a new one.
fieldNote: She connects office automation to **site pressure**, even though her own hands-on tasks change more slowly.
She has a conditional **union plan** and a specific trigger for applying to other crews.

steps.text: Ask the site steward about dues and join if affordable
Learn the contractor’s digital cutting sheets from foreman Mara
Apply to two repair crews after two thin rota weeks
Keep taking paid site days while the rota holds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my workmates the estimating desk changes in two years and our hands get maybe three more. We ought to ask for the timetable in writing, not take a promise in the canteen. I don't know which company would pay for human fitting after the robots work as well as us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I reckon the contractor could need fewer people to plan jobs by 2028. I might still carry and fit timber until around 2031, but that is only five years from now and I'd be 63. Five years of lower pay won't get my partner Elena and me to retirement safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask the union steward about membership and bring two coworkers to the meeting. I'd list our monthly bills with Elena and stop the paid television package, which is the first easy cut. During 2029, the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'd keep taking physical site work and ask the repair contractor for an interview if our firm cuts shifts. Before the 2031 robot date I'd ask the local college about a paid course in building inspection, but I could only enroll with funding or paid release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one makes my stomach drop. I can still make a plan on paper, but the paper doesn't make the next five years longer. Elena and I would both be awake after the lights go out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would the television money protect first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The electricity bill, because Elena's laundry uniform needs washing and the house needs heat. Our grown son lives on his own and pays his own rent; I wouldn't pretend he can carry ours. I'd rather ask him for a lift to a course than for cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay on the tools while looking at inspection. What makes the course possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The college would have to offer a funded place or my boss would have to pay me while I learned. I left school early and I'm still learning the trade, so I won't call myself an inspector after a weekend class. If neither offer appears, I'll keep applying for actual site work.

say: I would tell my **workmates** that office planning changes in 2028 and physical site work may follow around 2031.
I would ask the contractor for a **written timetable** instead of a canteen promise.
think: I may keep fitting timber until **2031**, but five years of low pay cannot secure retirement.
My partner and I lack the **cash** to coast through lost shifts.
do: Meet the **union steward** with two coworkers this month.
Cancel the **television package** and protect the electricity bill.
Apply for **site work** in 2029 if shifts fall.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about losing income before retirement and still see a narrow path to act.
S2.quote: Five years of lower pay won't get my partner Elena and me to retirement safely.
fieldNote: Aisha separates the **2028 desk change** from the 2031 arrival of capable hands-on robots.
Her son is financially independent, and she offers a **lift request** instead of treating him as a cash reserve.
The inspection course is **conditional** on funding or paid release; she does not claim instant qualification.

steps.text: Meet the union steward with two coworkers this month
Cancel the paid television package to protect the electricity bill
Apply to the repair contractor for site work if shifts fall in 2029
Enroll in building inspection only with funding or paid release

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew five years gives us room to ask for a real transition plan. The thinking work may go in 2031, but a machine that can fit and carry like us is dated around 2034. I want the union at the table before the purchases are signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when the thinking system arrives and 66 when the robots can do site work. That timing is cruelly close to retirement, but I have almost no savings now. I can imagine getting enough ordinary wages in between; I cannot assume it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start by asking the steward to take a five-year training and redundancy proposal to the contractor. I'd move thirty from full weeks into savings if the frame jobs keep coming and ask the college in spring about the funded inspection course. In 2032, the first year after AGI, I'd keep working on site and seek paid inspection training if my employer offers release; by 2034 I'd apply to maintenance teams if fitting hours disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less trapped than in the two-year picture, but I wouldn't call myself calm. Five years is enough to make calls, and also enough time for a bad winter to eat the plan. I find myself counting workdays in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the training proposal need to say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It needs paid hours for people who left school early, not just a link to an online course. I would ask for a clear sum if a job disappears and for priority on maintenance vacancies. Those are things the steward can actually put in a letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the contractor rejects that, what happens to your own savings plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still put thirty aside in full weeks, but I won't pretend every week is full. Elena and I would check the balance every month together. If a winter wipes it out, I'll keep seeking wages; I won't declare early retirement on an empty account.

say: I would press for a **transition plan** while five years remain before thinking AI arrives.
I would ask for **union involvement** before the contractor buys capable site robots.
think: I would be **63** at AGI and 66 when robots reach hands-on site work.
My nearly empty **savings** make retirement timing uncertain despite the longer warning.
do: Ask the **steward** to submit paid training and redundancy terms.
Put **thirty** aside after full weeks of work.
Seek **paid inspection training** in 2032 if the employer offers release.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with useful time to plan but no reliable cash buffer.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to make calls, and also enough time for a bad winter to eat the plan.
fieldNote: She wants **paid training hours** because early school leaving and junior standing make a quick credential implausible.
Even with five years, she refuses to equate a **savings intention** with money already in the bank.

steps.text: Ask the union steward for paid training and redundancy terms
Move thirty from each full work week into savings
Seek paid building inspection training in 2032 if released by employer
Apply to maintenance teams by 2034 if fitting hours disappear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my friends a ten-year warning is the first card that might let me finish working before the robot arrives. I'd be 68 when thinking AI comes and 71 when site robots can match our hands. That isn't a guarantee of retirement; the wage packets between now and then matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I know a long runway helps only if my body and the contractor's order book hold up. A robot around 2039 could still catch me working because we have less than one month's expenses saved. I don't want people to use my age as an excuse to ignore younger workers either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking paid carpentry shifts now and learn the contractor's material planning tool, because less waste might preserve jobs. I would also ask Elena to review our bills with me each quarter and set aside forty after full weeks, if the pay allows. In 2037, the first year after AGI, I'd still take physical building work if offered and ask the college about paid inspection training; if we have enough saved by the robot date, we could discuss retiring then, not promise it now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel a little relieved at having time, but not safe. Ten years is a lot of birthdays on a building site. I would rather use those years than spend them waiting for a cheque that may never come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop site work before 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need a real balance that covers our bills, not a birthday on a calendar. Elena's laundry hours are part time and move around, so I can't do the arithmetic alone. A doctor might also tell me my knees have had enough, which is another reason to learn before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a younger worker on the same crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to get the training agreement in writing while they have time. My plan may be to reach a paid retirement, but their plan needs years of work after 2039. The union should bargain for both groups, not just the old hands.

say: I would tell friends the **ten-year warning** may let me finish working before site robots arrive.
I would still say **wages matter** more than birthdays for retirement.
think: My **body** and the contractor’s orders must hold up for a long runway to help.
I could still need **site wages** when capable robots arrive around 2039.
do: Keep taking **carpentry shifts** while building work is offered.
Review **household bills** quarterly and save forty after full weeks when possible.
Ask the **college** about paid inspection training in 2037.
feel: I feel **relieved** by time but uneasy about ageing on site with little savings.
S4.quote: Ten years is a lot of birthdays on a building site.
fieldNote: Her possible retirement depends on a **real balance** and partner income, rather than on reaching an assumed age.
She explicitly includes **younger workers** in the training bargain, although her own runway is shorter.

steps.text: Keep taking paid carpentry shifts while site work is offered
Learn the contractor’s material planning tool to reduce waste
Set aside forty after full work weeks when pay allows
Ask the college about paid building inspection training in 2037

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most. It gives us just two years before the estimating changes and only until about 2031 before robots can match hands-on work. Paid training time, honest notice of lost shifts and a real payment if my job ends would help; a cheerful brochure wouldn't pay our electricity bill.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets the first chance at the training. A junior woman my age could be overlooked twice, once for being new and once for being old. I use AI every day, but I still need someone to let me learn the trade properly.

headlineQuote: A junior woman my age could be overlooked twice, once for being new and once for being old.
portrait: Aisha is a **58-year-old junior** construction worker who entered building work after a laundry closed.
She has **thin savings**, variable site hours and a partner whose part-time laundry shifts also vary.
She uses **AI daily** for material lists but checks every cut against her own measurements.
Her plans shift from **paid work** toward union terms, conditional training and savings as warning time grows.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** worries her most because desk work changes quickly and site robots follow around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **paid training**, honest notice of lost shifts and a concrete payment if her job ends.
